Of the 78 winners, 57 are returning to the same chamber, five are moving from the House to the Senate, and three are former members coming back. The 13 first-time entrants make up about one-sixth of the group. Much of the industry's successful electoral activity therefore preserved legislators with existing experience and positions.

The spending also reached most of these candidates well before November. Fifty received no supportive general-election spending from the five committees: 47 were backed only in 2026 primaries or runoffs, and three only in 2025 special elections.

Every first-time entrant received their support during a primary or runoff. These payments bought advertising and other election communications.

Under the Federal Election Commission's definition, independent expenditures advocate a candidate's election or defeat without coordination with the campaign or party. They are outside spending, rather than donations handed to candidates.

Backing someone in a primary can help determine which member of a party reaches the general election. That gives the committees an opportunity to influence the choices available in November, even when they spend nothing supporting the eventual nominee afterward.

Adrian Boafo and Jasmine Clark received the most support among the 13 first-time entrants: $5 million and $4 million, respectively, all from Protect Progress during their primaries. Together, they accounted for 67% of the $14 million spent supporting this newcomer group.

Their districts also offer a concrete way to assess what might change. Steny Hoyer, whom Boafo succeeds in Maryland's 5th District, voted against both the House's CLARITY market-structure bill and the GENIUS stablecoin bill in July 2025.

David Scott, who long represented Clark's Georgia district, voted against both as well. Boafo arrives with state legislation behind him. He sponsored Maryland's blockchain and digital-currency task force, established by a law approved in May. Its assignment is to study the technology's use and regulation, with recommendations due in October 2027.

He also sponsored a separate staking-services bill addressing restrictions and a securities exemption for qualifying services. The retrieved record shows a hearing, rather than enactment. His record gives the industry a reason to engage him on federal rules.

Clark's documented campaign commitments take a different form. Stand With Crypto's summary of her December 2025 questionnaire describes support for holding crypto in a personal wallet and for broad stablecoin availability.

The comparison with Scott requires one qualification: Everton Blair filled Scott's unexpired term after his death and is Clark's immediate predecessor. Scott's 2025 votes establish the district's earlier record on the two bills. They do not establish Blair's position or guarantee that Clark will vote differently on whatever text comes next. Both Boafo and Clark could change how their districts approach crypto legislation.

The largest spending effort in the review ended with the committees' preferred candidate losing. Defend American Jobs and Digital Freedom Fund reported $40 million supporting Husted and $24 million opposing Brown in Ohio's Senate election. Brown won.

The combined $64 million accounted for about 38% of the five-PAC total. It was almost as much as the approximately $64 million spent supporting all 78 eventual winners.

Shares of $168,134,698.98 in five-PAC reported candidate independent expenditures, 2025–2026 cycle, through Nov. 10, 2026, 08:37 UTC. The Ohio figure combines support and opposition spending; the winners figure includes support only. Both come from the reconciled five-PAC ledger for the same cycle and cutoff.

The Ohio effort puts the long winners list in perspective: one defeat accounted for an extraordinary share of the money. Brown was also one of seven candidates who won despite opposition spending from these committees.

The incoming Congress will include lawmakers the industry supported and others it spent heavily trying to defeat.

The winners divide evenly between the parties: 39 Democrats and 39 Republicans.

Their distribution across the chambers is much less balanced. Seven of the eight Senate winners are Republicans, with Virginia's Mark Warner the only Democrat in that group.

Democrats' victory in both chambers changes who will control committees and bring legislation forward. The overall bipartisan tally conceals how heavily the supported Senate roster leans toward the incoming minority.

This is a selected group of election winners, not a count of everyone who favors crypto legislation. CryptoSlate's earlier report on 241 winners rated favorably by Stand With Crypto used the advocacy group's assessments, a different measure from documented spending by these five PACs.

Neither tally includes every senator who will serve next year, since many were not up for election.

French Hill's reelection preserves an author of legislation the industry wants passed. The Arkansas Republican sponsored the House CLARITY Act, which would divide oversight of digital-asset markets between the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

He voted for that bill and GENIUS in July 2025, while Defend American Jobs and Fairshake reported a combined $1 million supporting him across the primary and general election.

Hill helped move CLARITY through the House on a 294–134 vote. He returns with that experience, although Democratic control will change the leadership of the Financial Services Committee he currently chairs. His next role and the compromises he will support remain to be determined.

Andy Barr brings a similar House voting record into a different chamber. The Kentucky Republican won a Senate seat after $8 million in supportive primary spending from Defend American Jobs and Fellowship. He voted for both House bills and chaired the Financial Institutions subcommittee in the outgoing Congress. His move gives the Senate a lawmaker who has already voted for a crypto market framework.

Warner demonstrates how far positions can diverge within the industry's own winners list. Fellowship reported $150,000 supporting his primary campaign. He voted for GENIUS in June 2025, then voted against advancing CLARITY in September 2026. In his explanation of that vote, Warner said the proposal lacked adequate restrictions on the president and senior officials profiting from crypto. He supported a federal regulatory framework while withholding support from legislation he considered deficient on ethics.

The September 15 vote was on cloture on the motion to proceed, a procedural step toward considering the bill. It failed 49–50. Warner's vote therefore records opposition to advancing that proposal at that stage, rather than rejection of every possible market-regulation bill. His position gives the industry a specific negotiating problem.

Agreement on stablecoins and a broader desire for federal rules can coexist with a demand for restrictions the bill's supporters have not accepted. Winning his seat again does nothing by itself to resolve that disagreement.

The legislation these lawmakers write, amend, and oversee could affect how an exchange handles your assets, how you redeem a stablecoin, and what you must calculate when filing taxes. Each area is at a different stage.

Exchange rules remain a legislative negotiation. The House CLARITY proposal would establish a federal framework for digital-commodity trading, including registration and customer-protection obligations.

The allocation of authority between regulators determines which rules a platform must follow and who enforces them. Hill has helped write that framework, Barr has voted for its House version, and Warner has identified conditions for advancing it in the Senate.

If the current Congress leaves the bill unfinished, it will need to be reintroduced in the next one. The election preserves experienced participants in that work, while leaving the actual agreement unresolved.

Stablecoin safeguards are moving into implementation. GENIUS became law in July 2025. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency finalized its implementing rule in October, with the law and that rule due to take effect on January 18, 2027.

Its reserve and redemption requirements concern the assets backing stablecoins and the process for getting dollars back. Other regulatory work continues: the Federal Reserve's September package contains proposals. Returning lawmakers will oversee implementation and may seek changes to the statute, so a vote for GENIUS does not settle every subsequent decision about issuers and their customers.

Tax relief has a supported lawmaker behind it, but remains a proposal. Steven Horsford received $1 million in general-election support from Fairshake and voted for both House crypto bills. The Nevada Democrat also joined the original sponsors of a digital-asset tax package that advanced through Ways and Means by 38–5 in September.

The introduced text of H.R.10357 includes simplified treatment of qualifying dollar stablecoins and a gain-and-loss exclusion for digital assets used to pay eligible network or transaction fees totaling $10 or less per underlying transaction. Someone paying such a fee with a token can currently have a disposal to account for, requiring its acquisition cost and value when spent. The proposal aims to remove that calculation for qualifying fees, rather than create a general exemption for small crypto purchases.

The package also pairs simpler accounting options with restrictions on claiming losses after selling and rapidly repurchasing substantially identical assets. The committee advanced a substitute, and the measure has not become law. Existing IRS obligations continue to apply.

Crypto's winning roster preserves lawmakers who have written bills and adds candidates with positions voters can now follow in office. Its political influence will become more tangible when those people decide which customer protections, tax provisions, and limits on officials' financial interests they are willing to put into law.

#5073. XRP ETFs Mark 1-Year Anniversary With 1.16 Billion XRP Accumulated

It has already been one year since the first U.S. ETF designed to provide exposure only to XRP officially began trading, when the XRP ETF market launched on November 14 last year.

Although XRP has not shown any impressive price growth, this marks a major milestone in its journey towards global expansion, especially greater institutional adoption.

While momentum has slowed significantly in recent days, data showcased by the official XRP X handle shows that the U.S. spot XRP ETFs have steadily expanded their holdings since they launched late last year.

As such, they have accumulated about 1.16 billion XRP to date, marking a major milestone for the broader XRP ecosystem even as momentum slows amid the prolonged market volatility.

While XRP ETFs are designed to allow investors to gain exposure to XRP through traditional means rather than by purchasing and holding the asset directly, the milestone signals growing interest in XRP investment products among institutional investors.

Nonetheless, the team shared a chart that revealed that XRP ETF holdings have generally trended upward since November 2025, with notable increases around the beginning of the launch period and another significant rise in August this year.

As the XRP ETF ecosystem continues to grow, the asset has seen several major asset managers join its ecosystem over the past year.

These asset management firms issuing the XRP investment product include Bitwise, Franklin Templeton, Canary Capital, 21Shares, Grayscale, and REX.

#5072. XRP Exchange Balances Hit Yearly High, but Long-Term Holders Stay Put

Home » Trendsetter News » XRP Exchange Balances Hit Yearly High, but Long-Term Holders Stay Put

XRP exchange balances have reached a one-year high, while the share of tokens untouched for over a year nears its annual peak.

XRP held on exchanges has reached a one-year high even as the share of coins untouched for more than a year approaches its own annual peak, according to figures cited by wealth-focused commentator Kamilah Stevenson.

Her latest video examines that split following a roughly 10% price decline, arguing that investors’ financial circumstances can matter as much as their market convictions.

Stevenson cites CryptoQuant data showing approximately 11.8 billion XRP on exchanges, the highest balance in a year. That puts more tokens within easy reach of trading, although exchange deposits alone do not establish that holders intend to sell.

Meanwhile, Glassnode figures cited in the video put the share of XRP unmoved for more than a year at roughly 56%, up from 51% in January. Stevenson also says XRP exchange-traded funds still hold about 1.19 billion tokens, despite a small outflow ending a reported 13-week inflow streak.

“Both groups saw the same price,” she says. “They reacted to it in completely opposite ways.”

The contrast is striking, but the metrics have limits. Coins remaining stationary demonstrate inactivity, not necessarily fresh buying or confidence, and neither measure establishes where XRP’s price goes next.

Dr. Stevenson identifies three recurring sources of selling pressure: leverage, investing money needed for near-term expenses, and entering a volatile market without a plan.

She cites roughly $25.7 million in XRP liquidations on Binance during a recent sell-off as an example of positions being closed regardless of investors’ intentions.

Her broader bullish case rests partly on institutional activity involving Ripple and its RLUSD stablecoin.

The YouTube video names Standard Chartered, Cross River Bank and DriveWealth among firms involved in custody, banking or settlement developments.

Those developments should not be treated as equivalent to demand for XRP itself. Nor does institutional infrastructure guarantee that token prices will recover.

The most durable point is about liquidity: cash reserves and manageable exposure reduce the likelihood that an unexpected bill or margin call dictates a sale.

Exchange balances may signal potential selling pressure across the market; they cannot reveal which holders can afford to wait.

#5070. Peter Schiff argues Bitcoin may fall below $16,500 by year-end if $50,000 breaks next

His Nov. 14 call extends earlier $20,000 warnings while Bitcoin and Ethereum traded above the conditions he identified.

Bitcoin critic and gold advocate Peter Schiff said on Nov. 14 that a Bitcoin break below $50,000 could send it toward a level below $16,500 before the end of 2026. The call extends his earlier downside warnings, while Bitcoin traded near $65,850 on Saturday afternoon.

In his 05:53 GMT post, @PeterSchiff said a break of $50,000 could lead to “a quick trip to the 2022 low below $16.5K.” He said a retest before year-end would not surprise him.

According to CryptoSlate data at 15:02 GMT on Nov. 14, Bitcoin traded at $65,850, down 4.36% over 24 hours. It was 47.82% below its Oct. 6, 2025 all-time high of $126,198.

Schiff’s latest post gives a more specific downside marker than his earlier warnings. On Feb. 19, @PeterSchiff said a break below $50,000 would make a test of $20,000 “highly likely.” On June 2, he said the same break should be followed by a quick fall below $20,000.

The November call retains that $50,000 condition while explicitly naming a level below $16,500 and a timeframe before year-end. His June wording already allowed for prices below $20,000, so it should not be read as having established a precise floor there.

Bitcoin and Ethereum remained above his first conditions in the Nov. 14 afternoon observations. The downside markers are his forecasts.

Observed prices had not crossed his first triggers in these snapshots; the year-end timeframe belongs to Bitcoin.

Personal forecasts do not establish future prices or historical-low accuracy. CryptoSlate observations are from 15:02 and 15:03 GMT on Nov. 14, not live updates. The Ethereum post did not state the Bitcoin year-end timeframe.

In a later Saturday post, @PeterSchiff argued that prospective buyers were already invested and that artificial intelligence had diverted attention from Bitcoin. He also alleged rising hacking risk and said the Trump-driven rally was over. Those were his explanations for expecting further weakness.

Peter Schiff attached a warning about Bitcoin-holding company Strategy to the forecast, saying a year-end retest would mean “curtains for $MSTR.” MSTR is Strategy’s listed common stock.

Strategy’s Nov. 9 filing reported holdings of 850,364 BTC as of Nov. 8, acquired for about $64 billion at an average cost of $75,456 per bitcoin, including fees and expenses. A lower Bitcoin price would reduce the market value of those holdings.

Schiff’s criticism of Strategy predates Saturday’s post. CryptoSlate reported in March on his objections to its preferred-stock funding model.

Ethereum traded at $1,851 at 15:03 GMT, according to CryptoSlate data, down 4.95% over 24 hours. It was 62.64% below its Aug. 24, 2025 all-time high of $4,954, but remained above the $1,600 level Schiff identified. The year-end timeframe appeared in his Bitcoin post; his Ethereum post described chart levels without assigning that same timeframe.

The immediate price test in Schiff’s argument is still $50,000 for Bitcoin. In the afternoon CryptoSlate observations, both Bitcoin and Ethereum remained above the respective trigger levels he cited.

#5069. Illinois Crypto Tax Draws Unlikely Alliance of DOJ, Banks and DeFi

Illinois Crypto Tax Draws Unlikely Alliance of DOJ, Banks and DeFi

An unusually broad coalition, spanning the U.S. Justice Department, Wall Street’s biggest lobby, the national Chamber of Commerce and a who’s-who of crypto firms, has thrown its weight behind a legal challenge to Illinois’ first-of-its-kind tax on digital asset transactions.

The groups filed briefs this month in Illinois state court supporting a lawsuit from the Crypto Council for Innovation and the Blockchain Association, which are asking a judge to strike down the state’s Digital Asset Tax Act and permanently block its enforcement.

The tax imposes a 0.2% levy on the full value of a digital asset every time an Illinois customer trades, transfers, or stores it through a broker, even when there’s no sale, gain, or change in ownership.

Critics have called it among the most punitive crypto taxes in the country, in part because Illinois imposes no comparable tax on dollars, gold, stocks or any other asset, and no other state has anything like it.

On Nov. 6, the Justice Department filed a statement of interest arguing the tax undermines federal policy and U.S. leadership in digital assets, calling it vague and discriminatory for singling out crypto for treatment no other asset faces.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, which represents hundreds of broker-dealers, banks and asset managers, filed an amicus brief warning the tax reaches well beyond crypto-native platforms to the traditional banks, custodians and advisers increasingly offering digital asset products.

A separate brief filed Nov. 11 brought together crypto’s heavy hitters, led by the DeFi Education Fund, Andreessen Horowitz, Paradigm and Uniswap, and including Aave Labs, Chainlink Labs, Solana Policy Institute, Phantom, Jito Labs, Multicoin Capital and Stand With Crypto.

Their filing argues the law’s definitions are so vague they could stretch to software developers and decentralized protocols that hold no customer funds and have no way to identify users or know where a transaction occurred. The brief noted an estimated 2.64 million Illinoisans hold digital assets, the fifth-highest total of any state.

“This tax is unclear, discriminatory, unconstitutional, and harmful to the future of finance,” CCI CEO Ji Hun Kim and Blockchain Association executive Ashok Pinto said in a joint statement.

The challenge dates to August. As Decrypt reported, Illinois agreed in October to pause the tax until July 1, 2027, buying time for the court fight now underway.

Cardano founder Charles Hoskinson has doubled down on his comments about completing the blockchain's development. In an AMA, the Cardano founder was asked about finishing Cardano; he answered in the affirmative, saying yes, the roadmap was done.

In a recent livestream titled "Finishing Cardano," Hoskinson maintains that his job with Cardano was done. "My job is done with Cardano," he said, doubling down on his recent statements and on where things stand with Cardano.

Finishing Cardano https://t.co/LtFVLOHrxk

Hoskinson said he saw a barrage of criticism and negative comments after his remarks, with some speculating that he had failed, that Cardano was a failed project, or that he was leaving Cardano. He, however, maintains that there is no ambiguity in his statements.

Hoskinson revisited the launch of Cardano (ADA) in 2015 in response to critics who claimed that he or the Cardano project had failed.

"So, let's look at 2015. There was a crowd sale conducted to sell ADA into Japan. The price for this was less than 0.2 cents per ADA. And Bitcoin was actually used as the settlement system for this. They bought in yen and settled in Bitcoin. So there are even on-chain records of the sales tranche. The total amount of money raised was $72 million."

Highlighting the growth of the Cardano cryptocurrency, Hoskinson noted that the market valuation has increased immensely from an initial $72 million. "We built a network that went from a $72 million valuation to an all-time high of $100 billion," Hoskinson stated.

Cardano reached an all-time high price of $3.09 on September 2, 2021, which corresponded to an all-time-high market capitalization of nearly $100 billion at that peak.

Following ADA's drop from this ATH, Cardano's market valuation sits at $6.03 billion. Hoskinson maintains that this is still growth, up from an initial $72 million. "Even in its deflated state, everybody's saying it's destroyed and it's a dead coin and all these other things. It's $6 billion. It went from 72 to six," Hoskinson said.

Hoskinson specifically reiterated that the Cardano roadmap is not being abandoned and went on to reveal further growth credentials: "We delivered a fully decentralized, recursively self-improving ecosystem. We left behind a community-led and community-owned treasury that, at its all-time high, had $4 billion in value, and initiated a constitution."

"We built an entire on-chain governance system, wrote a constitution, got the entire community involved, and created a recursively self-improving system that's fully decentralized—the most decentralized cryptocurrency on the planet," Hoskinson added.

For years, investors in the crypto market have followed a familiar pattern. The moment they see that Bitcoin’s price gains are eventually slowing down, they begin moving capital into Ethereum and other altcoins in search of higher returns.

This rotation has historically fueled what the market calls an “altcoin season.”

However, 2026 is beginning to challenge that expectation. Though the market has seen brief periods of outperformance, these have failed to develop into a sustained rally across the wider altcoin ecosystem.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the year is now approaching its end without a convincing sign of the long-awaited rotation.

To understand the case better first, let’s focus on the total altcoin market capitalization, which fell from approximately $1.85 trillion to $1.06 trillion in just a month, erasing almost around $800 billion in value.

At the same time, the Altcoin Season Index has struggled to maintain readings above the 75 threshold, which traditionally signals an altcoin season.

At press time, too, the index was sitting at 48, which means that the Bitcoin [BTC] season continues to be in full swing at the moment despite BTC trading at $73,836.99 at press time.

This came after a recent report by AMBCrypto, which indicated that the median altcoin’s returns by November had dropped slightly below Bitcoin and that both Bitcoin’s 60-day returns and the altcoin’s returns had returned to zero.

Going back in time, the years 2021 and 2023 delivered substantial rallies during different parts of the year. However, the year 2022 remained dominated by bearish sentiment. Moving forward, the end of 2024 is what provides an important point of comparison.

Following Bitcoin’s move above $100,000 in December, market attention expanded towards Ethereum [ETH], XRP, Solana, and other large-cap altcoins. And the broader market entered 2025 with considerable optimism around a potential continuation of that rotation.

However, the experience of 2025 also demonstrated that such rallies are not necessarily sustained. Glassnode’s historical analysis highlighted that altcoin trading volume had previously surged to nearly four times Bitcoin’s volume around September 2025, before cooling as Bitcoin approached its October market top.

The same pattern appeared in September 2026. Altcoin spot volume again climbed to almost four times Bitcoin’s volume, suggesting a period of heightened speculation. By late October, however, the ratio had declined to approximately three times Bitcoin’s volume.

He warned that major altcoins are approaching critical support levels. For instance, Hyperliquid [HYPE] could fall to $64 or $53 if it breaks below $75, while Ondo [ONDO] risks dropping to $0.26 or $0.19 below $0.35. Quant [QNT] could also decline towards $160 if it breaks below $190.

These setups suggest that selling pressure is spreading beyond smaller tokens, making a broad-based altcoin recovery increasingly unlikely in 2026.

Echoing a similar sentiment, another crypto educator on X added,

Using CryptoQuant analysis, he suggested that altcoins have lost approximately $200 billion in market capitalization. Around 70% of Binance-listed altcoins are trading below their 200-day moving averages, while only 13.2% of the top 250 crypto assets recorded positive returns in October.

Then, one of the strongest arguments against an imminent altcoin season is Bitcoin’s continued dominance. At press time too, Bitcoin dominance was around 60.98%.

That said, execs in the crypto communities are also increasingly questioning whether the traditional altcoin cycle is still relevant.

For instance, Benjamin Cowen, founder & CEO of ITC, in his recent commentary, added to this concern, where he argued that the arrival of Q4 highlighted the weakness across the market, with altcoins facing greater pressure.

Unfortunately, with the cryptocurrency market witnessing approximately $738.92 million in liquidations over the past 24 hours, affecting 120,474 traders according to CoinGlass data, concerns are valid.

Chainlink [LINK], Avalanche [AVAX], Litecoin [LTC], and Binance [BNB] also recorded smaller outflows. This suggests that investors were withdrawing capital across both Bitcoin and altcoins rather than rotating into smaller cryptocurrencies.

At the same time, the Crypto Fear and Greed Index was standing at ‘Fear’ at 29 at press time. These indicators reinforce one another and suggest that the traditional altcoin season is losing its momentum.

#5065. Binance Tightens Security With Zero-Knowledge Proof Upgrade

Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange by volume, has continued to deploy new measures to strengthen security on its exchange after it suffered the biggest cyberattack ever seen in the history of crypto late last month.

In a bid to foster transparency and regain its users' trust, Binance has just announced the completion of a major upgrade to further strengthen its security.

In an announcement shared on November 14, Binance said that it has generated a new zero-knowledge proof for its Proof of Reserves (PoR) system.

According to Binance, the upgrade allows users to independently verify that it holds sufficient assets to cover their account balances on a 1:1 basis.

The exchange further shared snapshots to prove that it maintains reserves above its users' net account balances across six major cryptocurrencies, boosting their confidence in its operating standards.

It also added that the update covers all assets affected by the recent attack, and the exchange showcased its reserves for the following crypto assets: Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tether, BNB, Solana, and USDC.

While withdrawals are being restored in batches, with the last phase scheduled for next week, Binance has continued to improve its operations to replenish all affected assets and tighten security to regain users' trust.

Following its latest move, Binance revealed that its Bitcoin reserves are currently at 100.05%, slightly above the 100% mark. This means that Binance's Bitcoin reserves amount to about 688,283 BTC, substantially above its net user balances of 687,912 BTC.

The case is similar for the rest of the tokens: Ethereum reserves are at 100.02%, while BNB and USDC recorded ratios of 100.39% and 100.07%, respectively.

While Binance also reported stronger reserve ratios for USDT and SOL, at about 104.34% and 105.86%, respectively, it is evident that Binance holds more of these assets than the total amount owed to users.

Binance has specified that the Proof of Reserves covers assets that are in its custody on behalf of users, rather than its entire corporate holdings, assuring users that their funds are fully backed.

Unlike simply holding Bitcoin, a leveraged long can be reduced or closed when a falling price erodes the collateral supporting it. A later rebound does not reopen a liquidated position.

#5063. What’s keeping Bitcoin buyers away despite 2 leverage flushes in 5 days?

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

On 29th October, the largest hack in crypto’s history took Bitcoin to a low near $76,200. A few days later, on 5th November, an AI-driven tech crash spilled into crypto. The Nasdaq 100 fell by 6.4%, while semiconductor stocks tumbled by 12%.

This chaos set off leveraged liquidations of roughly $1.1 billion and pushed Bitcoin’s price below $74,000.

Two different shocks, a historical Binance breach, and an AI token sell-off. Though they seem unrelated on the surface, this time they were actually the catalyst for the same event. What Bitcoin saw was a surge in speculative positioning, but what the king coin did not see was a buyer.

The market’s first take on the Binance hack was that crypto had passed a test. Bitcoin fell by about 6% from its 28th October close — a fraction of the 15% to 39% drawdowns after the controversies surrounding Celsius, FTX, BlockFi, and Bybit.

Matt Mena, Crypto Research Strategist at 21Shares, told AMBCrypto,

What we find most encouraging is how the market handled the worst of it. The largest hack in crypto’s history caused a far smaller drawdown than past crises; the protocols kept running, and none of the structural drivers broke.

Unfortunately, institutional resilience is not retail demand. The market simply treated a smaller slump as evidence of Bitcoin’s underlying strength. However, whether anyone wanted to buy Bitcoin [BTC] was a separate question, one the hack never answered.

Still, institutional strength hasn’t eased the feeling of dread felt by many retail investors. And, a major factor can explain why.

The most important signal is what happened after the liquidations: Nothing. Bitget Wallet’s analysts put it plainly that the leverage reset “has cleared some speculative excess, but is yet to address the underlying demand problem.”

Looking at the data, one can see why. Most importantly, the ETF flows changed drastically. There were $2.6 billion worth of inflows in September 2026, which turned into $290 million of net outflows in October. Currently, U.S ETF holders sit underwater below their cost basis of $82K.

How ETF holders behave below breakeven remains the key tell for November.

Also, stablecoin supply has not been moving outside the $305 billion zone, a sure sign that liquidity is sitting still.

Finally, one cannot forget the fallout caused by the Binance hack.

When the exchange reopened withdrawals, the queue moved fast. The exchange processed $4.65 billion against $1.01 billion of deposits in under ten hours; net outflows reached about $5.8 billion over 24 hours!

Each of these factors may not matter when seen separately, but when read together, they describe the same thing — capital leaving or sitting still. The leverage is gone, and the bid is not there to replace it.

For 21Shares, $73,000 is the 200-day moving average, and “the line that would reopen the bear-market debate.”

Bitget analysts told AMBCrypto that Bitcoin must hold the $73K–$74K range.

The 73,000-74,000 range is now the zone Bitcoin needs to hold. Stabilization would require more balanced derivatives positioning and sustained positive ETF flows. Reclaiming and holding $80,000 would signal stronger demand, while a decisive break below $73,000 could expose $68,000. If $68,000 also fails to hold, the selloff would suggest more than a temporary leverage flush.

When the same number pops up again and again, it stops being a coincidence and starts pointing to a pattern — that Bitcoin is either in a temporary flush or at the start of something deeper.

If buyers do return, Bitcoin can comfortably start holding $80,000, and stronger demand would emerge as a result. Getting back above $81,000 to $82,000 would finally put the largest holder cohorts back in profit.

Both reports are similarly aligned on what won’t fix Bitcoin’s buyer problem: Macro relief without demand. In fact, Bitget’s analysts asserted,

A durable Bitcoin recovery will depend on improving liquidity and Spot demand, not macro relief alone.

Matt Mena framed the same requirement as a four-part checklist.

We are watching four things into November: Bitcoin holding $76,000 to $78,000 and reclaiming $80,000 to $82,000, Binance completing withdrawals and proving its reserves, credit spreads, oil and long-end yields, and whether ETF flows return. If those turn, the setup for the final weeks of the year remains constructive.

Notice what’s on both lists: ETF flows, liquidity, Spot demand, and positioning. All of them are things buyers have to do.

There is naturally no doubt that macro factors can move Bitcoin’s price. If everything aligns, a rally can happen tomorrow. However, seasoned investors know that this will never be the same as rebuilding buyer interest.

Ultimately, a macro relief rally would leave Bitcoin’s demand problem exactly where it was.

The calendar offers a boost for Bitcoin regardless of which way the ball drops, as December’s Fed expectations hinge on U.S CPI and PPI readings. For the uninitiated, hotter readings will reinforce rate-hike expectations, and a softer core inflation will trigger a relief rally.

However, Bitget’s analysts draw a line between the two outcomes, noting,

This week’s inflation data adds another test. Hotter readings could reinforce December rate-hike expectations, while softer core inflation could trigger a relief rally. But a durable Bitcoin recovery will depend on improving liquidity and spot demand, not macro relief alone.

Basically, a relief rally can be classed as a macro event, not a demand event. The inflation print can only deliver the former, and the latter can only come about by real flows.

Here, it’s also worth being precise about what the 5th November AI crash tells us. 21Shares calls it,

A renewed wobble in artificial intelligence (AI) equities pulled the Nasdaq-100 down almost 4%.

That’s the mechanism in a nutshell. Even this time, crypto’s fall was the result of trading alongside a risk asset.

Still, if Bitcoin’s move below $74,000 was driven by the AI wipeout, then the absence of a bid is more telling. Eventually, we come back to the same problem of missing buyers.

Leverage has been reset twice in a week — Once by Binance’s $6.3 billion hack, once by an AI shocker. And the buyer bid has hardly appeared either time.

That’s what makes $73,000 a critical level to watch. If buyers return and hold this level, they could help Bitcoin reclaim $80,000. This would also imply that BTC’s demand problem is cyclical, not permanent.

However, a break below $73,000 will hint at — and a failure at $68,000 will confirm — that Bitcoin’s breakdown is structural. Bitcoin’s recovery hinges on a single level, and the lack of buyers has never been felt stronger.

Data from XRPL explorer Bithomp reveals that the Batch and Ticket features on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) are increasingly being adopted, with both setting new daily records in November.

The data indicates an increasing use of two XRPL features intended to enhance transaction flexibility and efficiency on the network.

Batch activity reached a new daily high for the month at 1.962 million on November 3, 2026. Ticket activity came next at 1.553 million on November 7, 2026, also setting a new November record. The increase indicates that these features are being embraced in the XRPL ecosystem. Batch functionality allows multiple transactions to be grouped and executed together and was activated on the XRPL mainnet on October 9, 2026.

The growth in batch activity, which neared 2 million on November 3, 2026, comes less than one month after its launch.

This is significant, as Batch is a prerequisite or accelerant for several high-value XRPL use cases already under contract or in the active pipeline, including atomic multi-party settlements. Institutional workflows (custody transfers, DvP settlement, cross-border payment finalization) require two or more accounts to act simultaneously.

On the other hand, tickets provide a way to reserve transaction sequence numbers, giving users more flexibility in managing transactions.

XRP Ledger metrics are in the green, with the transaction count up 75.9% to 4.3 million; active accounts jumped 128%, while XRP burned as fees rose 136%. Payments volume surged 137% in the last 24 hours to $1 billion, according to XRPScan data, while NFT mints rose 240% in the same timeframe.

Not only is the XRP Ledger seeing increased activity, but Ripple led stablecoin market cap growth by issuer over the past 24 hours, up $90.9 million, 4x the next issuer, multipli.fi, at $21.3 million.

Ripple's RLUSD market cap has grown 96% this year, across Ethereum and the XRP Ledger, to $2.7 billion from $1.4 billion in January. Most of that growth came in July, when Ripple launched Ripple Mint. RLUSD market cap stood just under $1.5 billion that month and rose to $2.3 billion by August.

In a milestone for the network, one year ago today, the first US ETF to hold only XRP began trading. Since then, US spot XRP ETFs have accumulated over 1.16 billion XRP.

Swift’s Spotlight on Speed report, released this week, shows that 50% of payments on its network now reach the recipient institution within 40 seconds, with 75% arriving within 10 minutes.

What will define the next generation of cross-border payments?The answer? More than just speed.Throughout @Sibos, conversations repeatedly focused on the customer experience. How do we make cross-border transactions more intuitive, more transparent and more predictable for… pic.twitter.com/yZoeZMDN4z

The cooperative noted that these figures put the industry ahead of the G20’s target for one-hour end-to-end processing by 2027 in the interbank leg of the journey.

The same report emphasizes that the “last mile”, the period after a payment reaches the receiving bank and before it is credited to the beneficiary’s account, still accounts for about 80% of the average end-to-end journey time.

Across 40 receiving markets analyzed, median last-mile processing sat near one hour in roughly one-third of cases, with wide variation between cross-border markets.

The conglomerate has called for greater use of one-leg-out models that connect international payments to domestic instant systems to reduce those final delays.

Digital Asset Investor’s reply to the Swift post was brief: “I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP.” The comment references the XRP Ledger’s typical ledger close time of roughly 3-5 seconds, which provides finality for on-ledger transfers.

I prefer 3-4 seconds. XRP. https://t.co/tBqXtEsqeM

In Ripple’s On-Demand Liquidity (ODL) model, XRP is used as a bridge asset so that currency conversion and settlement can occur without pre-funded nostro accounts.

End-to-end ODL flows that include exchange conversions have been described in the 3-5 second range for the core ledger step, though real-world completion including compliance and local payouts is often measured in seconds to a few minutes depending on the corridor.

The two claims are not measuring identical segments of a payment. Swift’s 40-second figure tracks time to the recipient institution, while the longer last-mile delays occur after that point.

https://t.co/ZA3CcggMOf @swiftcommunity @XRP @realfrandeolza @Archie_XRPL

XRP’s cited 3-4 second window refers primarily to ledger settlement of the bridge asset itself.

Traditional systems still handle the bulk of global bank-to-bank volume and benefit from established compliance and messaging standards; blockchain rails emphasize reduced pre-funding and faster finality on the asset transfer.

Whether the shorter settlement window on XRP produces a meaningfully better end-user experience continues to depend on how the on- and off-ramps, local banking rails, and compliance steps are integrated in any given corridor.

#5060. Why Binance’s ‘kill switch’ couldn’t stop hackers from draining $6.3B — Explained!

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

There is a certain irony in pulling the emergency brake, only to discover that the machinery you’re trying to stop is operating beyond your reach.

Binance encountered a rather expensive version of that problem on 29th October. Attackers compromised its wallet signing infrastructure and obtained authority to move cryptocurrency through mechanisms that did not depend on the exchange’s ordinary withdrawal process. Suspending withdrawals could interrupt that process. It could do considerably less about permissions already established on Ethereum.

By the time the attack was contained, approximately $6.3 billion had been stolen and Binance’s engineers had developed a specialised procedure to revoke malicious on-chain authority. The exchange could shut down affected services, but Ethereum would continue recognising the delegation until it was explicitly cleared.

Brian Cubellis, Chief Strategy Officer at Bitcoin custody platform Onramp, offered his two cents to AMBCrypto,

Pausing withdrawals turns off the exchange’s own software, but it does nothing about permissions the attacker has already written to the blockchain

The distinction is an uncomfortable one for an institution entrusted with billions in customer assets.

Binance subsequently coordinated freezes of stolen funds and began replenishing the affected holdings, reporting approximately 98% replenishment by 4th November. Its financial response was substantial.

However, it still is worth questioning what remained possible while its emergency controls were taking effect.

By the way, for those unaware, the attack began well before 29th October and nowhere near a blockchain.

According to Binance’s 3rd November incident report, an engineer downloaded a tampered installation package for an AI coding tool in June. The exchange detected the anomaly and replaced the device, but the attackers had already gathered intelligence about its employees and infrastructure. Well into September, another engineer was approached through a fictitious recruitment process involving interviews and a malicious coding assignment.

By 20th October, the attackers had used compromised employee systems and internal AI tooling to access additional machines. In doing so, they ultimately obtained credentials that opened the way to Binance’s wallet signing infrastructure.

It all paid off on the 29th. Between 20:05 and 20:09 UTC, hot wallets transferred approximately 223.46 million XRP, 970,500 SOL and 44.2 million OP to attacker controlled addresses. Bitcoin and other assets followed. Chainalysis subsequently estimated the overall theft at approximately $6.4 billion.

What was the most consequential part of this intrusion though? The attackers gained access to Binance’s signing infrastructure, the very machinery responsible for authorizing transactions.

On Ethereum, the attackers exploited EIP-7702, a mechanism that allows an externally owned account to delegate execution to smart-contract code.

Ordinarily, that flexibility expands what a wallet can do. Here, according to Binance, the compromised signing infrastructure was used to grant malicious code execution rights over an Ethereum hot wallet. The exchange described 50 signed transactions involved in manipulating the account’s nonce and establishing the delegation.

The unsettling part comes next though. Those permissions remained valid on-chain even after Binance suspended withdrawals and shut down its hot-wallet services. The exchange could stop its own systems from processing transactions, but it could not simply switch off the authority the attackers had already established on Ethereum.

Then came another complication. Binance’s hot wallet used multi-party computation (MPC), which distributes the production of cryptographic signatures across multiple participants or components rather than relying on a single conventional private key. That architecture can reduce certain risks, but it also meant there was no single private key available to revoke the malicious delegation immediately.

Binance’s engineers had to DEVELOP a specialised revocation procedure while the incident was UNFOLDING. Of course, this took additional time, prolonging the effort to contain unauthorized asset movements.

At 23:56 UTC, the final reported unauthorized Ethereum transfer, involving 2,961.9 ETH, was confirmed on-chain. Binance said it had been broadcast earlier and remained pending before confirmation. At 00:10 UTC on 30th October, the exchange cleared the malicious EIP-7702 delegation with a new authorization to the zero address.

The distinction between broadcast and confirmation matters. So does the absence of an established total for funds transferred after withdrawals were suspended.

Binance acknowledged that suspension alone could not stop every unauthorized movement, but its disclosures do not establish a reconciled post-suspension loss figure.

There is a comforting simplicity to the idea of a kill switch. Something goes wrong, someone pulls the plug and the damage stops. Unfortunately, the blockchain has no particular obligation to respect an exchange’s internal emergency procedures.

Consider a hotel discovering that someone has obtained an unauthorized key card. Closing reception prevents new cards from being issued. The existing card still opens the door. Cancelling it, securing the valuables, and recovering what has already disappeared are separate jobs.

Now, this comparison has its limits, but it captures the dilemma facing exchanges whose wallet permissions outlive their own systems.

The problem surfaced in a public exchange between Haseeb Qureshi, Managing Partner at Dragonfly, and  Tudor Anastasiu. Tudor Anastasiu is a blockchain infrastructure and security engineer and the founder of Anastasiu Labs.

The disagreement exposes a distinction that is easy to overlook in the middle of a breach.

A defensive sweep can move assets to safety, provided the exchange can authorize and execute it before the attacker does. However, moving funds does not necessarily invalidate permissions already granted on-chain and it certainly cannot retrieve assets that have already disappeared.

So, that leaves a rather awkward question: If the signing infrastructure itself has been compromised, how does an exchange authorize an emergency transaction without trusting the very system it suspects?

Carlos Vendrell, Founder of Zealynx Security, sees the answer in testing the procedure under exactly those conditions.

The drill should start from a list of every approval and delegation each hot wallet has given, then revoke one of them for real while assuming the normal signing service is the compromised part, and time it

Binance’s experience does not establish that MPC inherently prevents rapid revocation. Nor does its disclosure prove that no emergency procedure existed before the breach.

However, it does establish that engineers developed a specialised procedure during the incident and doing so took additional time.

There was another complication here, one that made the situation look almost absurd. The compromised wallet was reportedly STILL receiving money.

In an analysis dated 4th November, Four Pillars reported that Binance’s deposit-consolidation system continued collecting funds into a compromised Ethereum wallet identified as Binance 14. This allowed the attacker to sweep newly arriving assets.

Nexus Mutual’s reconstruction offers a particularly striking sequence.

At approximately 21:44 UTC, it says the attacker swept 200 million USDT that another Binance-labelled wallet had deposited roughly 72 seconds earlier. Seventy-two seconds! Barely enough time to make a cup of coffee, yet apparently sufficient for a fresh transfer to reach a compromised address and disappear.

The researchers’ findings raise a problem distinct from EIP-7702. An exchange can work to revoke an attacker’s authority while other operational systems continue directing funds towards a dangerous destination. Interrupting those internal asset flows is another containment task and requires its own controls and confirmation.

According to Brian Cubellis, emergency preparedness must account for the loss of the usual signing infrastructure.

An exchange should prove, before it is attacked, that it can cancel any permission on its wallets and move exposed funds to safety even if its own signing system has been taken over

That is easier prescribed than engineered though.

An independent emergency signing path may accelerate recovery, but it also introduces powerful authority that must be secured. Build too much dependence into the ordinary system and the emergency route may fail alongside it. Concentrate too much authority in the alternative and the supposed safeguard becomes another attractive target.

Once stolen assets leave the exchange’s immediate control, containment becomes a race involving investigators, stablecoin issuers, blockchain networks and the attacker.

Chainalysis’s investigation also described an attempt to move approximately $500 million in stablecoins through a swapping address. Within roughly 20 minutes, the attackers reportedly converted around $325 million into assets less susceptible to issuer freezes, including Ether. The remaining $175 million was frozen.

There was a reason for the rush. Stablecoin issuers such as Tether and Circle can freeze certain tokens at designated addresses. Bitcoin and Ether, by contrast, have no equivalent central issuer with that power. Converting the stolen stablecoins into other assets could therefore put them beyond the reach of an issuer-imposed freeze.

This whole episode illustrates the limits of intervention once funds have escaped. Investigators may be able to follow the money on-chain, but knowing where it has gone does not necessarily give them the power to retrieve it.

Binance nevertheless managed to secure a substantial portion of the stolen assets. In its 3rd November report, the exchange said that approximately $2.85 billion had been frozen or intercepted through cooperation with issuers, law enforcement, and blockchain intelligence firms. By 4th November, it reported replenishing approximately 98% of the affected holdings through replacement purchases.

Of course, Binance had demonstrated considerable capacity to absorb the losses rather than pass them on to users. However, it tells us how much the exchange managed to secure or replace, not how effectively it prevented the attacker from continuing to move assets during the breach.

A year earlier, Bybit had encountered a different version of the problem with compromised transaction authority. In February 2025, attackers stole approximately $1.5 billion after compromising the environment associated with its Safe{Wallet} approval process.

According to Bybit’s forensic disclosure, malicious changes deceived signers into approving an unauthorized transaction. It also said that investigators found no indication that its own infrastructure had been compromised.

Both incidents exposed how much depends on the integrity of the authority behind a transaction. Multiple signatures offer limited protection when signers are misled about what they are approving. And as Binance discovered, shutting down a signing service does not necessarily invalidate authority already established on-chain.

An emergency kill switch sounds reassuring. Rather less reassuring is discovering, halfway through a breach, that the attacker has permissions your switch cannot revoke.

Binance’s experience raises an uncomfortable question for exchanges entrusted with billions in customer assets — Have they actually tested what happens when the systems responsible for protecting those assets become part of the attack?

An exchange should be able to demonstrate that it can revoke compromised permissions, move exposed assets to safety, and interrupt internal transfers without relying entirely on infrastructure it can no longer trust.

But what should customers make of an exchange’s public assurances when a breach is underway? AMBCrypto put that question to Vik Sharma, Founder and CEO of Cake Wallet,

A useful update names which approvals were revoked, which assets moved, and where, so customers can check it themselves

There are legitimate reasons to withhold sensitive operational details while an intrusion is underway. Once the immediate danger has passed, however, an exchange should be able to explain what its emergency controls actually stopped, when compromised authority was extinguished, and whether any assets remained exposed.

Binance deserves credit for publishing details of its response, coordinating substantial asset freezes, and committing its own resources to replenish affected holdings. Those measures helped absorb the financial damage. However, they also revealed why reimbursement and containment should never be confused.

A kill switch should buy defenders control, not merely time to figure out where control has gone.

#5059. Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom: The AI Stock Winners and Losers After Jensen Huang’s Ousting

Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom: The AI Stock Winners and Losers After Jensen Huang’s Ousting

Wall Street is picking winners and losers from Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, and the market is treating the chipmaker's competitors considerably better than companies tied to its business.

Nvidia shares fell 4.59% to $165.75 Thursday afternoon, recovering from an opening price of $151.01 and an intraday low of $148.80.

The rebound softened an initial collapse of more than 14%, but the stock remained firmly in negative territory.

The selloff followed Huang's immediate resignation as CEO, president, and board member after reports of extramarital affairs and allegations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, although the company has not established that corporate secrets were compromised.

The stock was already in trouble before Huang stepped down. Nvidia had lost approximately $1.27 trillion in market capitalization between October 6 and November 6, raising questions about AI spending even before the leadership crisis intensified.

AMD climbed 5.79% to $584.89 after opening at $569.28, making it one of the clearest beneficiaries of Thursday's trading.

The company competes directly with Nvidia in AI accelerators, and uncertainty around Nvidia's leadership could make customers more interested in diversifying their chip suppliers.

Broadcom followed a similar trajectory, gaining 5.65% to $364.73 from an opening price of $356.80.

Unlike AMD, which competes through its own GPU products, Broadcom specializes in custom AI processors and networking technology, offering large customers a different way to reduce their dependence on Nvidia.

Google’s parent company Alphabet also advanced, rising 2.06% to $299.49 after opening at $293.77.

Those alternatives existed before Huang resigned, and Thursday's gains do not establish that Nvidia has lost customers. Investors may simply be pricing in better competitive opportunities if the leadership transition disrupts Nvidia's strategy or customer relationships.

Nvidia-backed CoreWeave suffered a much rougher session, falling 7.49% to $56.22 after opening at $50.91.

Its decline came just one day after the cloud provider surged 24.7% following quarterly revenue growth of 168%, so this may be just as much a correction after an explosive movement as it is a reaction to Huang’s ousting.

In any case, the relationship between the companies helps explain the anxiety among investors. Nvidia invested another $2 billion in CoreWeave in January and has an initial $6.3 billion agreement to purchase unused computing capacity through April 2032, making it an investor, supplier, and customer of the same company.

Any change in Nvidia's investment priorities could therefore affect CoreWeave beyond ordinary chip purchases, although neither company has announced changes to those agreements.

The pressure also reached the semiconductor supply chain. TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's advanced processors, fell 1.15% to $408.61 after opening at $394.62, while memory supplier Micron lost 2.70%, trading at $789.43 after opening at $769.31.

SK Hynix, another major supplier of high-bandwidth memory used in AI hardware, declined 3% to $137.98 from an opening price of $134.25.

These companies depend on broader chip demand, however, so their losses cannot be attributed entirely to Nvidia's leadership problems.

For investors, the immediate concern is less about whether AI chips will stop selling and more about how Nvidia manages its partnerships, financing commitments, and product roadmap without the executive who built much of that network.

Nvidia's board has said it expects operations and customer commitments to continue without interruption. The company is scheduled to report quarterly earnings on November 17, with Kress now leading the business through its first earnings announcement since Huang's departure.

#5054. Who Is Colette Kress, Jensen Huang’s Successor as Nvidia CEO?

Who Is Colette Kress, Jensen Huang’s Successor as Nvidia CEO?

For the first time in 33 years, someone other than Jensen Huang is running Nvidia. And the person taking over is not an engineer, a chip designer, or a Silicon Valley founder.

Colette Kress, Nvidia's 59-year-old chief financial officer, was named interim CEO Thursday following Huang's abrupt resignation amid reports of extramarital affairs and allegations involving a suspected Chinese intelligence operative.

Kress will remain CFO while the board searches for a permanent replacement, according to Nvidia's regulatory filing. She inherits a company worth trillions of dollars, a shaken investor base, and a management structure built around one man.

Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013, when it was primarily known for graphics cards used in video games. She arrived with nearly 25 years of financial experience across some of America's largest technology companies.

She spent eight years at Texas Instruments before joining Microsoft in 1997. During her 13-year tenure there, she became CFO of the Server and Tools division, overseeing financial strategy for Microsoft's enterprise computing business.

In 2010, she moved to Cisco as senior vice president and CFO of its Business Technology and Operations Finance organization, managing financial planning and business development across the networking giant's operations.

Kress holds a finance degree from the University of Arizona and an MBA from Southern Methodist University, according to her official biography.

Her move to Nvidia came with an unusual endorsement. Her two sons, then enthusiastic gamers, encouraged her to join the company responsible for the graphics chips powering their favorite games, according to Forbes.

Huang personally recruited her, explaining his vision for AI computing on a whiteboard during their discussions, Wired reported. At the time, Nvidia was the smallest company Kress had worked for.

When Kress joined Nvidia, its annual revenue stood at approximately $4.13 billion. By fiscal 2026, that figure had reached $215.9 billion, an increase of more than 50 times.

Huang drove Nvidia's technological strategy, but Kress oversaw the finances supporting its expansion from gaming hardware into data centers and AI infrastructure.

Her tenure included Nvidia's $6.9 billion acquisition of networking specialist Mellanox and an increasingly aggressive strategy of investing in companies that purchase its computing hardware.

Those relationships now include CoreWeave, in which Nvidia invested another $2 billion in January. CoreWeave's rapid growth reflects enormous demand for Nvidia-powered computing, alongside the financial costs of building that infrastructure.

Kress also became Nvidia's principal financial voice to Wall Street, regularly explaining margins, chip demand and revenue forecasts during earnings calls.

Forbes ranked her among America's richest self-made women in 2026, with almost $750 million in Nvidia shares as of Wednesday's close.

Kress takes charge as Nvidia faces questions about the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending. Nvidia had already lost approximately $1.27 trillion in market value from its October peak before the board publicly announced its investigation on Huang’s love affairs.

She must also navigate Washington's restrictions on advanced chip exports to China and scrutiny surrounding Nvidia's commercial relationships. The board has said it has no reason to believe company secrets or U.S. national security were compromised in the allegations involving Huang.

Her financial expertise cannot entirely replace Huang's technical background or his personal relationships with developers, customers, and governments. Maintaining Nvidia's engineering leadership will require close coordination with the executives responsible for its chips and software.

Kress has promised to build on Huang's legacy, saying that “Nvidia's strength has always come from its people.”

Her first major public test arrives Tuesday, November 17, when Nvidia reports its third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings. The company has scheduled its results for approximately 1:20 p.m. Pacific, followed by an investor call at 2 p.m.

#5047. Why the Path to Quantum Resistance Runs Uphill for Bitcoin Wallet Makers

Why the Path to Quantum Resistance Runs Uphill for Bitcoin Wallet Makers

Bitcoin custody has always involved some degree of risk, but wallet manufacturers like Trezor—which build physical devices designed to keep a user’s private keys secure offline—are preparing for a post-quantum world where new challenges arise.

That’s because SHRINCS, the community’s leading candidate for a post-quantum signature scheme, allows users to make transactions using stateful signatures that require rigid state tracking to prevent funds from being stolen, according to Trezor CTO Tomáš Sušánka.

Proposed late last year by Blockstream Research Director Jonas Nick and cryptographer Mikhail Kudinov, SHRINCS centers on a composite hash-based approach: users can make transactions using either stateful signatures or stateless signatures.

Stateless signatures are quite large—potentially affecting fees, signature speed, and other efficiency metrics—but are safe to reuse, while smaller, more efficient stateful signatures come with serious security risks when reused beyond a particular signing budget.

The stateful component of SHRINCS is made up of a tree of one-time signatures, and if these keys are accidentally used more than once, enough cryptographic information is revealed for someone else to forge that user’s signature and effectively steal funds.

If Bitcoin successfully adopts SHRINCS, maintaining a meticulous count of the wallet’s state will become a critical responsibility for wallet developers—with lots of potential edge-case security risks.

“You’re giving them an option to mess up,” Sušánka said during a recent episode of MARA Foundation TV, in reference to state tracking. “It’s our job to make it in a secure way, right? It shouldn't be the user’s job.”

To mitigate this risk, Trezor is weighing options for how to support secure UX in a post-quantum world. For instance, Sušánka said the company is considering making the heavier, slower stateless signatures the default setting for all users, tucking the riskier stateful option behind an advanced settings wall.

While Sušánka recognizes that SHRINCS may be the conservative cryptographic choice because it relies on the same cryptographic assumptions as SHA-256, he is “kind of torn on the topic because maintaining the state is a burden.”

“For example, you can have two Trezors with the same recovery seed. How do you share the state between those two? You really don’t,” he added.

“That being said, as it is with everything, this is about trade-offs,” Sušánka continued. “The [stateful] signatures are 10 times smaller ... That makes a big difference. So, I just don't want to throw it off the table completely.”

Sušánka went on to share that while many are focused on Bitcoin’s migration path to post-quantum addresses and signatures, hardware wallet devices will also need to be physically updated for full quantum protection. Most signing devices use quantum-vulnerable cryptography for hardware-specific security functions, like firmware and device authentication.

If users want to ensure their devices are secure in a post-quantum world, they will need to use “quantum-ready” devices—that is, devices that use post-quantum cryptography for device and firmware authentication as well.

In anticipation of these needs, the company is already shipping products like Trezor Safe 7 that support post-quantum cryptography for wallet authentication processes. Of course, transactions made on these devices will only be quantum-secure once Bitcoin itself upgrades to post-quantum security.

That said, Sušánka warned developers not to wait too long to give users migration options, as he believes the migration of potentially millions of users will take time.

“People should be ready to make compromises,” Sušánka said. “If we’re all going to be very strict on what can and cannot be done, we’re not going to get anywhere.”

André Beganski is a Senior Content Manager at MARA Foundation, producing content on topics including the intersection of quantum computing and cryptography. He has previously worked for Decrypt.

#5042. Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy Made $19.5 Billion in Profit. So Why Is MSCI Removing It From Stock Indexes?

Strategy made $19.53 billion in profit last quarter. Yet MSCI, one of the world’s biggest providers of stock indexes, has decided Michael Saylor’s Bitcoin company no longer belongs in some of its major investment benchmarks.

MSCI’s November review lists “STRATEGY A”—the company’s MSTR shares—for deletion from the MSCI USA Index after trading closes November 30. That also removes the stock from broader indexes that include U.S. companies, such as the MSCI World and MSCI All Country World indexes.

That sounds technical, but the distinction matters: MSCI is not removing Strategy from the Nasdaq stock exchange, shutting down its business, or making it sell Bitcoin. It is taking MSTR out of stock lists that investment funds use to decide which companies to own.

Consider an ETF designed to copy the MSCI USA Index. When MSTR disappears from the list, the fund generally has to sell its shares, regardless of whether the fund manager likes Saylor’s strategy.

This is why it’s bad news for Strategy. It means less indirect exposition to investments.

MSCI adopted new rules in October for so-called non-operating companies. The idea is to keep investment vehicles—businesses that mainly hold financial assets—out of indexes meant to track operating companies. Its screening process considers a company’s operating assets and other financial measures.

MSCI’s deletion list does not spell out exactly which tests Strategy failed. The company, however, argues that raising capital, managing its Bitcoin treasury and issuing financial products amount to a genuine operating business.

In an August letter to MSCI, Strategy called the proposal “discriminatory, arbitrary, and misguided.” It argued that MSCI should be a “mirror of the market, not an arbiter of it.”

Strategy also maintains a software business, but Bitcoin now dominates its finances. The disagreement is whether its Bitcoin activity counts as running a company or mainly managing an investment portfolio.

Strategy’s latest quarterly earnings show $19.53 billion in net income. But that does not mean its software customers paid the company anything close to that amount.

Nearly all of its $20.91 billion in reported operating income came from a rise in the accounting value of its Bitcoin. Under rules adopted in 2025, changes in Bitcoin’s market price appear in Strategy’s earnings even when it has not sold the coins. A decline in Bitcoin can produce the opposite result.

Its software division, meanwhile, recorded $125.4 million in quarterly revenue, down 3% from a year earlier. Its $477.2 million in revenue for all of 2025 was slightly below the $486.3 million reported in 2019, before Strategy began buying Bitcoin.

The immediate risk is selling pressure on MSTR, not on Bitcoin itself. Strategy estimated that funds linked to MSCI indexes hold roughly 13 million of its shares, or 3.1% of its outstanding common stock. Not all of that necessarily translates into sudden sales, and Strategy says the amount is manageable.

But Strategy has repeatedly raised money by selling shares and other securities, then used those proceeds to buy Bitcoin. If its stock falls, selling the same number of new shares brings in less cash.

So the company would have to issue more shares to raise the same amount—or buy fewer Bitcoin.

That is why a stock-index decision could eventually matter to the crypto market. The exclusion does not force a Bitcoin sale, and it does not guarantee fewer purchases. It could, however, weaken a key source of funding for one of Bitcoin’s biggest corporate buyers.

The International Energy Agency raised its fourth-quarter 2026 oil supply forecast by 3.3 million barrels a day in its November 13 report and now expects a quarterly surplus. The improved outlook could reduce oil-related inflation pressure, which matters to Bitcoin through interest rates and investors' willingness to take risk.

The upgrade follows an October supply increase of 2.3 million barrels a day to 105.4 million, as Gulf exports recovered faster than demand. The IEA projects a larger inventory build in 2027. The 3.3 million figure is an increase in its supply forecast, not the size of the expected surplus.

Observed global inventories rose by 52 million barrels in October, the IEA reported. Oil on water, a component of the global total, increased by 86 million barrels, while on-land stocks continued falling and reached their lowest level since at least 2016. OECD total stocks declined by 47 million barrels.

The IEA's November outlook pairs a projected Q4 surplus with October inventory gains concentrated at sea.

The IEA raised expected Q4 2026 supply by 3.3 million barrels a day and projects a quarterly surplus.

Gulf product and LPG exports remained around half pre-war levels; European diesel was 77% above pre-war prices at the IEA's time of writing.

Broader prices still matter: the Bureau of Labor Statistics' October CPI release showed consumer prices rising 0.4%, energy 0.7% and prices excluding food and energy 0.3%, all on a seasonally adjusted monthly basis.

The Federal Reserve held its policy-rate target at 3.75% to 4% on October 28 and said inflation remained elevated. In a November 13 speech, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson said energy costs were feeding into airfares and transportation and warned about persistent broader inflation. He identified inflation's trajectory as the more important policy signal, while keeping future adjustments dependent on the data.

Bitcoin's connection runs through financial conditions and willingness to take risk. A 2023 IMF working paper found that U.S. monetary tightening reduced a common component of crypto-price movements through the risk-taking channel, resembling the effect on equities.

For Bitcoin, the potential relief depends on oil reaching refineries and cheaper fuel easing broader inflation. Rebuilt land stocks and recovering fuel exports would help; renewed shipping attacks or stubborn inflation could keep the pressure on.
